unit.title: Protect self against communicable diseases in the workplace

summary: This unit teaches you how infectious diseases spread and how a beauty therapist protects herself from them at work. You will learn the main kinds of germs and the common diseases in Jamaica, good hand hygiene, protective equipment, vaccines and healthy habits, and what to do after a cut or splash of blood. You will also learn how to guard against mosquito, rat, water and food hazards, and what to do when you or a client is ill.

blocks.p: A beauty therapist works very close to people: her hands are on their skin, her face is near theirs, and she handles blades, tweezers, wax and towels that touch blood, sweat and broken skin. That makes salon and spa workers more likely to meet germs than many other workers. This unit is about protecting **yourself**. The unit on infection prevention and control looks at protecting clients and keeping the salon clean; here the focus is on you, your health and your habits.

It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees. A therapist who is often sick, or who passes an infection to her family or to a client, harms her own health, her income and the salon's name. Most of what protects you is simple: clean hands, protective equipment, vaccines, covering cuts, rest, clean water and food, and staying at home when you are ill.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: a walk-through check for disease risks with a staff poster, and a drill on hand hygiene, PPE and what to do after an exposure. The assessor watches your method, your safety and your teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In group practical work, photograph only hands, papers, posters and equipment. Do not photograph a member's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it. Never use real blood or real sharps in drills.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **communicable disease** (also called an infectious or contagious disease) is an illness that can pass from one person to another, or from an animal or insect to a person. A **pathogen** is a germ that can cause disease. Germs are too small to see without a microscope, so you must work as if they are always present.

head: Germ
What it is
Examples that matter to you
Treatment
rows: Bacteria
Tiny single-celled living things. Many are harmless; some cause illness.
Impetigo, boils, tuberculosis (TB), tetanus, leptospirosis
A doctor may give antibiotics.
Viruses
Even smaller; they can only multiply inside living cells.
Colds, flu, COVID-19, hepatitis A, B and C, HIV, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, chickenpox, cold sores
Antibiotics do **not** work. Vaccines can prevent some; a doctor may give other medicines.
Fungi
Moulds and yeasts that like warm, damp places.
Ringworm, athlete's foot, fungal nail infection
Antifungal creams or tablets from a doctor or pharmacist.
Parasites
Small creatures that live on or in another living thing and feed from it.
Head lice, scabies mites
Special lotions from a pharmacist or doctor.

blocks.note: Antibiotics kill bacteria only. Taking antibiotics for a cold or flu does not help and can make germs resistant, so that antibiotics stop working later. Take them only when a doctor says so, and finish the course.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A disease passes along a chain of links. If you break any link, the disease cannot pass.

flow: The germ (pathogen)
Where it lives (a person, animal, water or surface)
The way out (cough, blood, wound, faeces)
How it travels (the route)
The way in (mouth, nose, eyes, cut, bite)
A person who can catch it (susceptible)

head: Route
How it happens
Examples in or near the salon
rows: Through the air (droplets)
An infected person coughs, sneezes or talks close to others; droplets are breathed in or land on the eyes, nose or mouth. Some germs float in the air for longer.
Colds, flu, COVID-19, TB, chickenpox
Direct contact
Skin touches skin, or a sore or lesion.
Scabies, impetigo, head lice (head to head), cold sores
Indirect contact
Germs left on an object (towel, comb, tool, handle) are picked up by the next person.
Ringworm, conjunctivitis, impetigo, colds
Blood and body fluids
Infected blood or fluids enter through a cut, broken skin, the eyes or the mouth.
Hepatitis B and C, HIV, from a used blade or a blood splash
Food and water (the faecal-oral route)
Germs from faeces reach food or drink, often by unwashed hands, flies or unsafe water.
Hepatitis A, typhoid, many stomach bugs and diarrhoea
Animals and insects (vectors)
A bite from an infected insect, or contact with water or soil soiled by infected animals.
Dengue, chikungunya and Zika (mosquitoes); leptospirosis (urine of rats and other animals)

head: Word
What it means
rows: Carrier
A person who has the germ and can pass it on, but shows no signs of being ill.
Incubation period
The time between catching a germ and the first signs of the disease. You can sometimes pass it on during this time.
Vector
An insect or animal, such as a mosquito, that carries a germ from one living thing to another.
Immunity
The body's ability to fight off a disease, from having had it or from a vaccine.
Outbreak
More cases of a disease than expected in one place or group.
Epidemic
A disease that spreads quickly to many people in one area.
Pandemic
A disease that spreads across many countries.
Endemic
A disease that is always present in an area at a steady level, as dengue is in Jamaica.
Isolation
Keeping a person who is sick away from others so that they do not pass the disease on.
Quarantine
Keeping a healthy person who may have been exposed away from others, in case she becomes ill.
Contact tracing
Finding and warning the people who were close to someone who has an infectious disease.

blocks.h: Why salon and spa workers are at risk

ul: You work within arm's length of clients, often face to face, for long periods.
You touch skin, nails, hair and sometimes broken skin, and handle tools that cut or pierce.
Towels, gowns, couches, chairs and door handles pass from client to client.
You deal with many people each day, some of whom feel unwell but come anyway.
Long hours, missed meals and too little sleep lower your resistance.

sections.title: Common diseases that affect salon workers

blocks.p: You do not diagnose or treat disease; a doctor does. But you must know the main diseases, how they spread and what the warning signs look like, so that you protect yourself and know when to send someone to a doctor.

head: Disease
Cause
How it spreads
Warning signs
How you protect yourself
rows: Colds and flu
Viruses
Droplets; hands and surfaces
Runny nose, sore throat, cough; flu adds fever, aches and tiredness
Wash hands, cover coughs, ventilate, do not share items, vaccine for flu, stay home when ill
COVID-19
A virus
Droplets and close contact in poorly ventilated rooms
Fever, cough, loss of taste or smell, tiredness
Ventilation, hand hygiene, masks when advised, vaccine, follow Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance
Tuberculosis (TB)
Bacteria
Droplets from someone with TB of the lungs
A cough lasting more than two to three weeks, night sweats, weight loss, tiredness
Good ventilation; see a doctor for a long cough; follow the doctor's treatment fully
Chickenpox
A virus
Droplets, and contact with the blisters
Itchy rash that turns to blisters, fever
Stay away from work while infectious; vaccine; avoid contact if you are pregnant or have not had it
Dengue, chikungunya, Zika
Viruses
Bite of the Aedes mosquito
Fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, rash, severe joint pain (chikungunya); Zika may be mild but can harm an unborn baby
Remove standing water; screens; repellent; cover skin
Leptospirosis
Bacteria
Water, mud or soil soiled by the urine of infected animals, mainly rats; enters through cuts or the eyes, nose and mouth
Fever, headache, muscle pain, red eyes, jaundice (yellow skin) in severe cases
Boots and gloves in floods; cover cuts; control rats; see a doctor early
Hepatitis A
A virus
Food and water soiled with faeces
Tiredness, nausea, yellow skin and eyes, dark urine
Hand washing, safe food and water; vaccine is available
Hepatitis B and C
Viruses
Blood and body fluids; used blades
Often none at first; later tiredness, yellow skin, liver damage
Standard precautions, sharps box, covered cuts; **hepatitis B has a vaccine**
HIV
A virus that attacks the immune system
Blood, sexual fluids, breast milk; not by everyday contact
Often none for years; later frequent illnesses (AIDS)
Standard precautions, never share blades or needles; a test and treatment are available in confidence
Impetigo
Bacteria
Direct contact and shared towels
Weeping sores and honey-coloured crusts
Do not touch sores; wash hands; see a doctor
Ringworm (tinea)
A fungus
Skin contact; shared towels and combs
Round, scaly, itchy patches
Gloves, clean tools, see a pharmacist or doctor
Scabies
A mite
Close skin contact; shared towels and bedding
Very itchy rash, worse at night, between fingers and on wrists
Avoid contact; treatment for all close contacts
Head lice
An insect parasite
Head-to-head contact; combs and hats
Itchy scalp; live lice or nits (eggs) on the hair
Do not share combs or brushes; treat as a pharmacist advises
Conjunctivitis ('pink eye')
Viruses, bacteria or an allergy
Contact with discharge; shared towels or eye make-up
Red, sticky, watery eyes
Do not rub eyes; wash hands; own towel; see a doctor
Tetanus
Bacteria in soil and dust
Through cuts and deep wounds, not from person to person
Stiff jaw and muscles
A tetanus vaccine and booster; clean cuts at once

blocks.note: Do not rely on how a client or co-worker looks. A person with hepatitis B or HIV can look and feel completely well. That is why you use the same precautions with every person, every time.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Dengue, chikungunya and Zika are endemic or common in Jamaica, and flu, colds and other diseases rise and fall through the year. The Ministry of Health and Wellness issues alerts. Follow the guidance it gives, not social media posts.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Protecting yourself: hands, PPE and daily habits

blocks.p: Clean hands are the single most important protection. Most germs reach your body on your hands, when you touch your eyes, nose or mouth or eat.

head: Method
When to use it
How
rows: Soap and water
When hands are visibly dirty or soiled, after the toilet, before eating, after blood or body fluids
Remove rings and watch; wet hands with clean running water
Apply liquid soap; rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips and wrists for at least **20 seconds**
Rinse well; dry with a clean single-use paper towel
Use the towel to turn off the tap
Alcohol hand rub
When hands are not visibly dirty, between clients and tasks
Use a rub with at least 60% alcohol
Cover all surfaces and rub until dry (about 20 seconds)
Do not rinse or wipe

ul: Before and after every client
Before putting on gloves and after taking them off
After touching blood, body fluids, broken skin, used tools or soiled laundry
After coughing, sneezing, blowing your nose or touching your face
After using the toilet; before preparing or eating food; after handling waste
After touching shared surfaces such as door handles, phones and the till

blocks.note: Wearing gloves does not replace hand washing. Germs can reach your hands when you take gloves off, and gloves can have tiny holes. Always clean your hands after removing them.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Care of hands, nails and skin

ul: Keep nails short, clean and smooth. Germs hide under long nails and in nail products.
Take off rings, bracelets and watches before work with clients.
**Cover every cut, graze or sore** with a waterproof plaster, and wear gloves over it when you handle clients.
Dry your hands well and use hand cream, so that the skin does not crack. Cracked skin is a way in for germs. Report sore or weeping skin on your hands to your supervisor and a doctor.

head: PPE
Protects against
Use it when
rows: Disposable gloves
Contact with blood, body fluids, chemicals and broken skin
Waxing, extractions, cleaning tools, dealing with spills, handling used items, giving first aid
Disposable apron
Splashes onto your uniform and skin
Cleaning, working with chemicals or any task likely to splash
Mask
Droplets from the mouth and nose, and dust and fumes
Treating a client who is coughing (if you must), during outbreaks when advised, filing nails or mixing powders
Eye protection (goggles or visor)
Splashes into the eyes
Mixing or pouring disinfectant, cleaning, tasks where blood or liquid could splash

blocks.h: Putting on and taking off PPE

flow: Wash your hands
Put on the apron
Put on the mask
Put on eye protection
Put on gloves last, over the cuffs
After the task, take off the gloves first without touching the outside
Remove eye protection and mask by the straps, then the apron, rolling it inwards
Put used items in the correct waste
Wash your hands again

ul: Use **new gloves for every client** and change them if they tear. Never reuse or wash disposable gloves.
Take off gloves by pinching the first glove at the wrist and peeling it off inside out. Hold it in the other gloved hand. Slide a clean finger under the second glove and peel it off over the first.
Choose gloves that suit the task: a chemical-resistant type such as nitrile for disinfectants. Some people are allergic to latex; use latex-free gloves if you or a client reacts.

head: Habit
Why it helps
rows: Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or the bend of your elbow, bin the tissue, then clean your hands
Stops droplets landing on people and surfaces. Hands carry germs to everything you touch.
Do not touch your eyes, nose or mouth with unwashed hands
These are ways in for germs.
Use your own cup, plate, towel, razor, tweezers and make-up brushes
Germs pass on shared items.
Wear a clean uniform each day, and tie back long hair
Germs and dirt collect on cloth and hair through the day.
Keep your work area and workstation clean; clean and disinfect shared surfaces often
Door handles, phones, card machines and taps are touched by many hands.
Open windows, use fans and extractor fans
Moving air carries germs away from the breathing zone.
Do not eat, drink or smoke in the treatment room
Germs and chemicals can get from your hands to your mouth.
Wear closed, non-slip shoes that you can wash
Protect your feet from spills and sharp items.

blocks.p: A **vaccine** teaches your body's immune system to recognise a germ without making you ill with the full disease. If you meet the germ later, your body fights it off quickly. Vaccines do not cure a disease you already have. They protect you, and they help protect clients, co-workers and your family, because a protected person is less likely to pass the germ on.

head: Vaccine
Why it matters to a beauty therapist
Notes
rows: Hepatitis B
You may meet blood from cuts, blades and broken skin.
Usually a course of three doses over about six months; a doctor may check later that it worked. Ask your doctor or health centre.
Tetanus (with diphtheria, as a booster)
Tetanus germs in soil and dust enter through cuts.
Boosters are needed every ten years or after a dirty wound; ask your doctor.
Influenza (flu)
You work close to many people; flu viruses change.
Given each year, because the viruses change.
COVID-19
Close work with many people.
Follow the Ministry of Health and Wellness advice on doses and boosters.
Hepatitis A, measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), chickenpox
Protects you if you were not vaccinated or have not had the disease.
Ask your doctor or health centre about your childhood vaccination record.

ul: Keep a copy of your vaccination record, and ask for a replacement at the health centre if you have lost it.
In Jamaica, vaccines and advice are available at **public health centres** and from doctors. Some are free; some may cost money.
Speak to your doctor if you are pregnant, have an illness or have had a bad reaction to a vaccine before. Vaccines are your own medical decision, made with advice from a doctor.

blocks.note: Vaccines are not 100% effective, and they do not replace hand washing, PPE and standard precautions. Use all the protections together.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Habit
How it protects you
rows: Eat regular, balanced meals
A body that is well fed fights infection better; skipping meals leaves you tired and weak.
Drink clean water through the day
Water keeps you hydrated in Jamaica's heat, and helps the body work.
Sleep enough, usually seven to nine hours
Sleep restores the immune system.
Manage stress and take breaks
Long-term stress and too little rest make it easier to catch infections.
Move your body and stand well
Exercise builds general health and reduces fatigue.
Do not smoke, and drink alcohol sparingly
Smoking damages the lungs and makes chest infections worse.
Go for check-ups and treat illness early
Early treatment stops infections spreading and getting worse.

blocks.p: Blood-borne viruses, mainly **hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV**, pass when infected blood or certain body fluids get into another person's body through a cut, broken skin, the eyes or the mouth. In a salon, the risk comes from used blades, cuticle nippers and tweezers that draw blood, blood on towels and surfaces, and cuts on your own hands. The risk is small if you follow the rules, and large if you do not.

**Standard precautions** (also called universal precautions) mean treating **all** blood and body fluids as if they could be infectious, from every client, every time. You cannot tell by looking who is infected.

ul: Clean your hands often and wear the right PPE.
Cover your own cuts and grazes with a waterproof dressing.
Use single-use blades and discard them at once into a **sharps box** (a rigid, puncture-proof, labelled container). Never recap, bend or break a used blade, and never pass one from hand to hand.
Clean and disinfect or sterilise reusable tools as the policy says; throw away single-use items.
Deal with blood spills at once with a spill kit and the correct disinfectant.
Put waste soiled with blood into clinical waste bags, not the ordinary bin.
Do not share razors, tweezers, nail clippers or toothbrushes.

blocks.h: What to do after an exposure

blocks.p: An **exposure** is a cut or needle-stick from a used sharp, or a splash of blood or body fluid in your eye, mouth or on broken skin.

head: Exposure
What to do straight away
rows: Cut or prick from a used blade or tool
Let the wound bleed gently; do not suck it or scrub it
Wash it well with soap and running water
Cover it with a waterproof dressing
Blood or fluid splashed into the eye
Rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean running water or eyewash for several minutes
Do not rub it
Splash into the mouth
Spit it out and rinse the mouth well with water several times; do not swallow
Blood on unbroken skin
Wash the area with soap and water

flow: Make the area safe and look after the client
First aid as in the table above
Tell your supervisor at once, even if you feel fine
Get medical advice the same day: a doctor, health centre or hospital
Complete the incident report
Follow the doctor's advice on tests, vaccines and treatment, and keep appointments
Keep the matter private

blocks.note: After some exposures, medicine to prevent infection (post-exposure prophylaxis) works best if it is started quickly, within hours and no later than about 72 hours. You will not know if you need it unless a doctor decides. That is why you must get medical advice quickly, even if the wound looks small.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Report and record** every exposure: date, time, what happened, where, which tool or fluid, and, if known, who was involved. The record protects you and helps the doctor.
If the client may have been exposed to your blood, the salon policy tells you what to do. Do not decide this alone.

head: HIV is spread by
HIV is NOT spread by
rows: Unprotected sex
Sharing needles, blades or other sharps
Infected blood entering a cut or the eyes
From mother to baby, in pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding
Shaking hands, hugging or sharing a room
Sharing cups, plates, towels or toilets
Coughs, sneezes or mosquito bites

blocks.p: A person living with HIV who takes treatment can stay healthy for many years and can reach a state where the virus can no longer be passed on sexually. Testing is available in confidence, and treatment is available through public health services.

blocks.note: If a co-worker or client tells you that she is living with HIV, or any other health condition, **keep it private** and treat her as you always do. It is her information. Telling others, refusing to work with her or asking for her to be moved is wrong. The workplace HIV policy says that status is private and that no worker may be treated unfairly because of it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Dengue, chikungunya and Zika are spread by the **Aedes aegypti** mosquito. This mosquito lives close to people, lays its eggs in clean standing water in and around buildings, and bites mostly **in the daytime**, especially early in the morning and in the late afternoon. It is a small mosquito with white markings on its legs.

flow: A female mosquito lays eggs on the wall of a container just above the water
Rain or water covers the eggs and they hatch into larvae (wrigglers)
Larvae become pupae and then adult mosquitoes in about a week
A mosquito that has bitten a sick person carries the virus
She bites another person and passes the virus on

head: Where it breeds
What you do
rows: Drums, tanks, buckets, barrels
Cover them tightly; scrub the sides weekly
Old tyres, cans, bottles, bottle caps, plastic containers
Throw away, or store them upside down or under cover
Flower pots, plant saucers, vases
Empty and scrub the saucers weekly, or remove them
Blocked gutters, drains and puddles
Clear them so that water flows
Waste bins and skips
Keep bins lidded; have waste collected regularly
Air-conditioner trays, water coolers
Empty and clean them weekly

ul: **Search and destroy** at least once a week: look inside and around the salon, the yard and the staff room for anything that holds water.
Use screens on windows and doors; use insect repellent on bare skin as the label says, and wear light clothes that cover arms and legs during the day.

If you have a fever, headache and pain behind the eyes, see a doctor. Drink plenty of fluids. Do **not** take aspirin or ibuprofen for suspected dengue unless a doctor says so, because they can increase bleeding; paracetamol is the usual choice. Follow the doctor's advice.
Zika can harm an unborn baby. Pregnant workers and clients should take extra care to avoid bites and talk to a doctor.

blocks.p: **Leptospirosis** is caused by bacteria in the urine of infected animals, mainly **rats**, and also dogs, pigs, cattle and mongooses. The bacteria live in water, mud and wet soil, and enter the body through cuts and broken skin, or through the eyes, nose and mouth. It is common after floods and heavy rain.

ul: After floods, wear **rubber boots and gloves** to clear mud and debris, cover any cuts with waterproof dressings and wash your hands and arms with soap and clean water afterwards. Do not walk barefoot in flood water or wade through it when you do not need to.
Do not swallow flood water or use it to wash food, dishes or the salon's tools.
Keep rats away: store food in sealed containers, use bins with tight lids, clear rubbish, block holes and gaps, and do not let water or food lie around.
See a doctor early if you have fever, headache, muscle pain or red eyes within about 2 to 30 days after contact with flood water, and say that you were exposed. Early treatment works best.

head: Hazard
What you do
rows: Unwashed hands
Wash hands with soap and water before preparing or eating food, and after the toilet
Food left out
Cover food; keep cooked rice, meat and milk products in the fridge soon after cooking; throw away anything past its date
Flies, ants, cockroaches and rats
Cover food, wipe spills at once, keep bins lidded and emptied daily
Dirty cups, plates and cloths
Wash in hot soapy water; dry in clean air; change cloths often
Unsafe drinking water

Use water from a safe supply. When the authorities advise it, or if you doubt it, bring water to a **rolling boil for at least one minute**, let it cool and keep it covered in a clean container; or use bottled water. Do not use plain tank or drum water if it may be contaminated.
Shared fridge and microwave
Label and date food; clean the fridge regularly

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat spoils food quickly. Do not leave cooked rice, chicken or fish on the staff room counter for hours. Keep it cold or eat it soon after cooking, and throw out what is left.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: When someone is ill: policy, reporting and responsibilities

blocks.p: Working while infectious puts clients, co-workers and your family at risk. Follow the salon's **sickness policy** and the advice of your doctor.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Fever, cough, sore throat or flu symptoms
Stay at home; tell your supervisor as early as you can; see a doctor if it lasts or you have trouble breathing
Vomiting or diarrhoea
Stay at home until you are well, usually until 48 hours after the last episode, or as your doctor or the policy says; wash hands often
Weeping, infected or spreading rash, especially on the hands
Report it, see a doctor and do not work on clients until you are cleared
Red, sticky eyes
Stay home or follow the policy; do not share towels or make-up
Illness with a rash, such as chickenpox
Stay at home until the doctor says you are no longer infectious
Illness during the working day
Tell your supervisor, go home, cover coughs and wear a mask if near others

ul: Do not treat a client who is coughing, sneezing, feverish or has an infectious skin condition. Explain kindly, offer to rebook when she is well and suggest she sees a doctor.
Clean and disinfect surfaces, chairs and tools she touched, and wash towels hot.
Do not guess at her illness or tell others about it. Record only what you saw and what you said.
Get your information from the **Ministry of Health and Wellness** and your parish health department, not from social media.

Follow its advice on masks, distancing, ventilation, cleaning, isolation and quarantine. **Isolation** is for people who are ill; **quarantine** is for people who may have caught the disease but are not yet ill.
If you are asked for information for contact tracing, give it truthfully. It is used to protect people, and it is kept confidential.
Notify the manager at once if you or a client has a notifiable disease; some diseases must be reported to the health authorities.

head: The employer or the Centre
You, the worker
rows: Provides a safe workplace and a written infection control and sickness policy
Trains staff and supplies soap, hand rub, paper towels, PPE, sharps boxes and spill kits
Keeps the premises clean, ventilated and free of pests
Gives information about vaccines
Lets sick workers stay home and keeps health information private
Follows the policy and training
Uses PPE correctly and cleans her hands
Covers her cuts and keeps her vaccines up to date
Reports illness, exposures, hazards and damaged equipment
Does not come to work while infectious
Respects others' privacy

blocks.note: Employers have a duty to provide a safe and healthy workplace, and workers must cooperate. Ask your instructor about the Centre's policy and the current law.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can define communicable disease, pathogen, carrier, incubation period, epidemic, endemic and pandemic.
I can name the four kinds of germ and give an example of a disease each causes.
I can explain why antibiotics do not work against viruses.
I can describe the chain of infection and the ways germs spread, with an example of each.
I can describe the cause, spread and warning signs of the common diseases that affect salon workers.
I can wash my hands properly and say when to wash with soap and water and when alcohol rub is enough.
I can choose PPE for a task and put it on and take it off safely.
I can describe the daily habits that protect me: covering cuts, nails, clean uniform, coughs and sneezes, not sharing items.
I can explain how a vaccine works and say which vaccines I should ask my doctor about.
I can say how sleep, food, water and stress affect my resistance.
I can explain standard precautions and why every client is treated the same way.
I can say what to do straight after a cut from a used blade or a blood splash, and why I must report it.
I can say how HIV is and is not spread, and how a worker living with HIV must be treated.
I can describe how to prevent dengue, chikungunya and Zika, and where Aedes mosquitoes breed.
I can describe how to protect myself from leptospirosis after a flood.
I can describe how to keep food and drinking water safe.
I can say what to do when I am ill, when a client is ill, and during an outbreak.
I can explain the employer's and the worker's responsibilities.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I let the wound bleed gently and wash it with soap and water, because this helps to flush out germs; I report it the same day because treatment works best when it is started early.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Communicable disease
An illness that can pass from one person, animal or insect to another.
Pathogen
A germ that can cause disease.
Bacteria
Tiny single-celled living things; some cause illness; antibiotics can treat them.
Virus
A germ smaller than bacteria that multiplies inside cells; antibiotics do not work on it.
Fungus
A mould or yeast that causes infections such as ringworm.
Parasite
A creature that lives on or in another living thing, such as head lice or scabies mites.
Carrier
A person who has a germ and can pass it on without showing signs of illness.
Incubation period
The time between catching a germ and the first signs of the disease.
Vector
An insect or animal that carries a germ from one living thing to another.
Immunity
The body's ability to fight off a disease.
Epidemic
A disease that spreads quickly to many people in one area.
Endemic
A disease always present in an area at a steady level.
Pandemic
A disease that spreads across many countries.
Isolation
Keeping a sick person away from others.
Quarantine
Keeping a well person who may have been exposed away from others.
Contact tracing
Finding and warning the people who were close to an infected person.
Standard precautions
Safe steps taken with every client, treating all blood and body fluids as possibly infectious.
Personal protective equipment (PPE)
Gloves, aprons, masks and eye protection that protect the worker.
Sharps box
A rigid, puncture-proof, labelled container for used blades and needles.
Blood-borne virus
A virus carried in blood, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
Exposure
A cut or prick from a used sharp, or a splash of blood in the eye, mouth or on broken skin.
Post-exposure prophylaxis
Medicine given quickly after an exposure to try to prevent infection.
Vaccine
A product that trains the immune system to fight a germ.
Aedes mosquito
The mosquito that spreads dengue, chikungunya and Zika; it breeds in clean standing water and bites by day.
Leptospirosis
A bacterial disease from water or soil soiled with the urine of infected animals, mainly rats.
Sickness policy
The workplace rules on reporting illness and staying away from work while infectious.
Incident report
A written record of an injury, exposure or accident.

c1.title: A coughing client in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: Mrs Cecile Francis, a regular client at a spa in Savanna-la-Mar, arrives for a one-hour facial. She is coughing, her eyes are watery and she says she has had a fever since Sunday. She also says she does not want to lose her booking fee. Therapist Dwayne has a new baby at home. The treatment room has no window, and the fan is switched off.

c2.title: A nick from a blade in Morant Bay
c2.text: While removing blackheads, therapist Kimberly nicks her own finger on a used lancet. The glove tore at the fingertip. The client, Mr Orville Henry, says he 'had hepatitis years ago' but is not sure which type. Kimberly feels fine and wants to finish the treatment, because the next client has arrived and the salon is busy. The salon has a sharps box, spill kit and incident book.

c3.title: Standing water behind the salon in Portmore
c3.text: After a week of rain, a trainee, Jodian, finds an old tyre, a bucket and three bottle caps full of water behind a salon in Portmore. Two plant saucers in the staff room also hold water. A co-worker, Tashane, has a fever, headache and pain behind her eyes and wants to take ibuprofen. The owner says she will spray the yard 'when she has time'.

c4.title: Flood clean-up in Old Harbour
c4.text: A river overflowed and flooded a salon in Old Harbour. The staff must clear mud and debris from the back room the next day. Latoya has a cut on her hand, and Marlon wants to work in his slippers to keep his shoes clean. Water is also running through the staff kitchen. A rat has been seen near the bins.

c5.title: A staff room and a sick co-worker in Montego Bay
c5.text: At a spa in Montego Bay, staff keep cooked rice and chicken on the staff room counter from 8 a.m. until lunch. One shared towel hangs by the sink, and the tap water has been brown for two days. Therapist Camille has had vomiting and diarrhoea since last night but says she cannot afford a day off.

c6.title: A confidential disclosure in May Pen
c6.text: Therapist Sharon tells her co-worker Delroy, in confidence, that she has HIV and takes treatment. Another therapist, Pauline, overhears and says the salon should not let Sharon do waxing or nails. Delroy is unsure what to say. He is also not sure whether he has had the hepatitis B vaccine.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do about Mrs Francis's facial?
o: Explain kindly that it cannot go ahead today, and offer to rebook
Give the facial, but wear a mask and gloves throughout the whole treatment
Give a shorter facial and leave out the steam to reduce the risk
Ask her to sit in the waiting area until her cough settles, then start
questions.why: A client with a cough, fever and watery eyes may have an infection that spreads by droplets. Following the policy, you postpone the treatment kindly and rebook; a mask or a shorter treatment still keeps you close to her for an hour.

questions.q: The treatment room has no window and the fan is off. Why does that matter?
o: Germs only survive in dark rooms, so a window would have let in light
The fan would have made the facial products dry out too quickly on her skin
A closed room makes clients cough more because the air is too dry
Droplets hang in still air, so moving air helps to carry them away
questions.why: Moving air carries droplets away and dilutes them. Open doors and windows and use fans or an extractor fan when you can, because poor ventilation leaves germs around you.

questions.q: Mrs Francis coughed into her hand and then touched the couch rail and the card machine. What should Dwayne do after she leaves?
o: Spray air freshener in the room and wipe the card machine dry with a tissue
Wipe the couch with a damp towel and use the same towel on the next couch
Open the door, clean then disinfect what she touched, and wash his hands
Leave the room closed for an hour so that the germs die off by themselves
questions.why: Germs left on surfaces pass on by indirect contact, so clean then disinfect what many hands touch and clean your own hands. Air freshener hides smells and kills nothing.

questions.q: Dwayne has a new baby at home. What is the best thing for him to do when he reaches home?
o: Put on a mask and hold the baby as usual, since the mask protects her
Wash his hands and face and change out of his uniform first
Wipe his hands on a dry towel and go straight to the baby for a cuddle
Hold the baby only after he has eaten dinner and rested for a while
questions.why: Germs travel home on your hands, hair and uniform, and babies are at special risk. Washing and changing first breaks that link; a clean uniform each day also helps.

questions.q: Kimberly has nicked her finger on a used lancet. What should she do first?
o: Let it bleed gently, wash it with soap and running water, then cover it
Suck the wound to draw out any germs, then cover it with a plaster
Squeeze it hard and scrub it with bleach to be sure any germs are killed
Finish the treatment first, then wash the cut at the next quiet moment
questions.why: Letting it bleed a little and washing with soap and running water helps flush germs out. Sucking, scrubbing or using bleach can make the injury worse, and delay lets germs stay in the wound.

questions.q: After first aid, what is the next step?
o: Wait a week to see whether she feels ill before telling anyone
Ask Mr Henry to take a blood test on the spot to settle the matter
Carry on and mention it to the owner at the end of the week
Tell the supervisor, record it and see a doctor the same day
questions.why: Every exposure must be reported and recorded, and a doctor must see it quickly, because preventive treatment and tests work best when started early. The doctor, not the therapist, decides what is needed.

questions.q: Why should Kimberly not wait to find out which type of hepatitis Mr Henry had?
o: The doctor will only see her once the client's test results have come back
Mr Henry is bound to give a wrong answer, so his answer is not useful
Treatment works best if started early, and a carrier may not know
Hepatitis can only be caught on the day of the treatment, not later
questions.why: Blood-borne viruses can be present without signs, and clients may not know or may forget their history. Standard precautions mean that every exposure is treated seriously and checked promptly.

questions.q: Why does it matter that Kimberly's hepatitis B vaccine course is complete?
o: It makes her immune to every disease passed on by blood
It means she no longer needs to wear gloves
It lets the doctor judge her protection and what to do next
It allows her to carry on working without reporting the injury
questions.why: The hepatitis B vaccine protects against one blood-borne virus only, not HIV or hepatitis C, and it does not replace gloves or reporting. Her vaccine record helps the doctor decide what follow-up she needs.

questions.q: The owner says she will spray the yard when she has time. Why is spraying alone not enough?
o: Spray kills only some adults; eggs and larvae in standing water remain
Spraying always makes the water dirtier, so more mosquitoes breed there
Mosquitoes only breed in the staff room, where the plant saucers are
Spray cannot be used near people in daylight, so it must wait till night
questions.why: Aedes mosquitoes breed in clean standing water in small containers. Removing or covering the water stops them breeding; spraying kills adults for only a short time.

questions.q: Tashane has a fever, headache and pain behind the eyes, and wants ibuprofen. What should she do?
o: Take ibuprofen and carry on working until the evening, then rest
Take aspirin instead of ibuprofen, because it is a stronger painkiller
Wait until the fever has lasted a week before seeing a doctor
Rest at home, drink fluids and ask a doctor before taking medicine
questions.why: These are signs of dengue. Aspirin and ibuprofen can increase the risk of bleeding, so a doctor should decide; paracetamol is the usual choice. Early medical advice matters.

questions.q: Why should Tashane also try to avoid mosquito bites while she is ill?
o: Mosquito bites make dengue last longer in the same person who is infected
Bites will push her fever higher and keep it up for several days
A mosquito that bites her may pick up the virus and pass it on
Bites cause the pain behind her eyes, so avoiding them eases it
questions.why: Mosquitoes are vectors: a female that feeds on an infected person can carry the virus and infect the next person she bites. Screens, a net and repellent protect everyone.

questions.q: Why is it unsafe for Marlon to clear flood mud in slippers?
o: Slippers are not slip-resistant, so he may fall in the mud and hurt himself
Bare skin in mud and water lets leptospirosis germs in, so he needs boots
Slippers will let mosquitoes bite his feet while he works near the water
Mud may spoil his slippers and then he would have to buy a new pair
questions.why: Leptospirosis bacteria from animal urine live in flood water and mud and enter through cuts and broken skin. Rubber boots and gloves, and covered cuts, protect you. Slips are another risk, but the infection is the main danger here.

questions.q: Latoya has a cut on her hand. What is the best choice for her?
o: Cover it with a waterproof dressing under gloves, or do other work
Leave it uncovered so that it dries in the sun and heals faster
Rinse it with the flood water to clean it before she starts work
Put on a plaster and work in the mud with her bare hands as usual
questions.why: Cuts are an entry point for germs. A waterproof dressing under gloves, or other work, keeps flood water away. A plaster alone is not enough in mud, and flood water is never clean.

questions.q: Flood water ran through the staff kitchen. What should staff do with the open food and the cups?
o: Rinse the cups under the tap and keep the open food in the fridge
Wipe the food containers dry and carry on using them after lunch
Boil the open food for a few minutes and then it is safe to eat
Throw away the open food; wash and disinfect the cups with safe water
questions.why: Flood water carries germs from sewage and animals. Food and drink that touched it should be thrown away, and hard items cleaned, then disinfected, with safe water.

questions.q: Why is it unsafe to leave the cooked rice and chicken out from 8 a.m. until lunch?
o: The food will go dry and lose its taste and goodness
Flies are only attracted to food at lunch time, not earlier
Germs multiply quickly in warm food and can cause illness
Chicken should always be reheated in a microwave before it is eaten
questions.why: In Jamaica's heat, bacteria grow very fast in cooked food left out. Keep cooked food covered and cold until it is eaten, and throw away what is left.

questions.q: The tap water has been brown for two days. What should staff do?
o: Drink it, as brown water is only rust and cannot cause illness
Use bottled water or boil tap water for a minute, and report it
Drink it after adding a little perfume or lime juice to freshen it
Let the water stand in a jug for an hour and then drink it
questions.why: Brown water may be contaminated, and discoloured water can carry disease. Use safe water until the supply is clear, and tell the manager so that the authorities can be told.

questions.q: What should Camille do about her vomiting and diarrhoea?
o: Stay at home until she is well, and tell her supervisor
Come in but work at reception, away from the treatment rooms
Take antibiotics from a friend and come back to work tomorrow
Come in and keep her hands washed and wear gloves all day
questions.why: Vomiting and diarrhoea can spread to co-workers and clients, especially by hands and food. She should stay home until she is well, and the salon's policy should make that possible. Antibiotics do not treat most stomach illnesses.

questions.q: Pauline says the salon should not let Sharon do waxing. What should Delroy say?
o: That Sharon should be moved to another salon for everyone's safety
That Sharon must wear double gloves and a mask for every client
That Pauline should tell the owner and let her decide what happens
That her health is private and HIV is not spread by everyday work
questions.why: HIV is not spread by everyday contact. Standard precautions protect everyone, and a worker's status is private. A workplace may not treat a worker unfairly because of it.

questions.q: Delroy is not sure about his hepatitis B vaccine. What should he do?
o: Assume that his childhood vaccines must have covered it already
Ask Sharon, because she knows most about blood-borne viruses
Check his record and ask a doctor whether he needs the course
Wait until he has a cut at work and then decide what to do
questions.why: Hepatitis B vaccination protects workers who may meet blood. Check the record and ask a doctor or health centre before an exposure happens, not after.

questions.q: A therapist who is pregnant, and has never had chickenpox, learns that a client she treated today has it. What should she do?
o: Nothing, since chickenpox is only a children's illness
Avoid further contact and speak to her doctor promptly
Put on a mask and carry on working as normal
Take antibiotics to prevent infection
questions.why: Chickenpox can be serious in pregnancy and for the unborn baby. She should speak to her doctor soon, and the salon should follow its policy. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
